source.title: Are Larger Pretrained Language Models Uniformly Better? Comparing Performance at the Instance Level
source.authors: Ruiqi Zhong; Dhruba Ghosh; D. Klein; Jacob Steinhardt

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream task accuracy across BERT sizes and correlations between instance-level accuracy changes across successive size increases. It does not measure pretraining cross-entropy or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling-law work and mentions prior correlations between language-model loss and downstream performance, but those cited findings are not its own results. Its own relevant results are the downstream accuracy comparisons and instance-level improvement correlations recorded below.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (BERT models of five sizes, pretrained by the authors, fine-tuned on QQP, MNLI and SST-2), the study reports in-distribution downstream accuracy for each size (Table 8). Accuracy rises monotonically with size on every task. No curve is fitted and no prediction is made from pretraining loss. This bears only weakly on V6. The paper's main results (instance-level decay, momentum, variance) are about instance-level behaviour, not about how predictable aggregate performance is.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that larger pretrained BERTs have higher average accuracy but are worse on a nontrivial fraction of instances (at least 1–4%), that instance-level improvements show momentum across successive sizes, and that fine-tuning variance grows with size. They recommend that researchers release model predictions alongside model weights.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares downstream classification accuracies and instance-level prediction behavior across fine-tuned BERT sizes; it does not measure held-out language-model loss or fit the original scaling-law recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported correlation depends on model-size gap; correlations are higher for the smaller-gap SMALL–MEDIUM–BASE triplet than for MINI–MEDIUM–LARGE.

fits_no_version.finding: Despite higher aggregate accuracy, LARGE is worse than MINI on at least ~4% of MNLI instances under the rigorous bound (1–4% across tasks), against a 2–10% aggregate gain. Larger size gaps give larger decaying fractions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains from scale are not uniform across instances: a nontrivial fraction of instances get worse as model size grows.

fits_no_version.finding: Instance-level accuracy gains are positively correlated across successive size steps once conditioned on middle-model accuracy (momentum). The correlation is weaker for larger size gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Instance-level improvements from scaling show momentum across successive size increases.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning-seed variance grows with model size (0.036→0.043 on MNLI) and is 2–8× pretraining variance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger pretrained models have higher fine-tuning variance at the instance level.

record.problems: The study does not measure pretraining loss or fit scaling curves. The BERT models use context size 128 rather than 512 and 2M pretraining steps rather than 1M; the authors report MNLI performance 2∼3% below the original release for BASE and LARGE. Table 6 does not report uncertainty for the correlations.
record.rows_left_out: The separate instance-decay lower-bound results in Table 2 and Table 9, and additional correlation results in Appendix G, were not extracted as rows for V6 because they report instance-level decay fractions or additional correlation conditions beyond the selected Table 6 correlations and overall-accuracy comparisons. The study also evaluates out-of-distribution/challenging sets; these are not represented in the extracted in-distribution accuracy table.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss is never measured or fitted.
Depth and width vary together with size; there is no comparison at fixed parameter count.
Fine-tuning is used, but no power-law form is fitted for it.

No functional form is fitted to accuracy versus size, there is no prediction from pretraining loss, and parameter counts are not reported. Out-of-distribution accuracies (SNLI, HANS, STRESS, TwitterPPDB) are evaluated but not reported as numbers.

missing.what: Averaged Bias² of 0/1 loss falls monotonically with size on MNLI (0.203, 0.179, 0.157, 0.134, 0.111). This is a downstream error measure across five sizes.
The standard deviation of overall accuracy across seeds is 0.2–0.3% per size. This gives uncertainty for the Table 8 accuracy rows.

record.verdict_notes: Table 8 is a sanity check (Appendix B) comparing the authors' checkpoints with the originals, but it still reports the study's own monotone accuracy-versus-size results. The record's limits_scope label based on momentum size-gap dependence is dropped: momentum is an instance-level construct, not V6's aggregate predictability. Parameter counts are not stated, so 'predictably with scale' cannot be assessed quantitatively. The authors' checkpoints differ from the original BERT pretraining recipe (context 128, 2M steps).

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on small runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their scaling with compute.
Architecture effects on pretraining loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.

The study measures downstream accuracy across BERT sizes and correlations between instance-level accuracy changes. It does not test prediction from held-out pretraining loss, fit quantitative scaling curves, or evaluate extrapolations to much larger models.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup or fitting choices; bending of loss curves.

rows.operation_detail: Correlated estimated instance-accuracy improvements across successive model-size increases, conditioned on middle-model accuracy.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation coefficient between SMALL→MEDIUM and MEDIUM→BASE estimated instance-accuracy improvements
rows.note: The paper reports positive conditional correlations across the listed buckets.
rows.check: This is an instance-level correlation of accuracy gains across successive size steps (momentum). It does not measure whether aggregate downstream performance improves predictably with scale, so it is a related but different construct.

relationships.condition: In-distribution fine-tuned accuracy on QQP, MNLI and SST-2, MINI→LARGE, both author-pretrained and original checkpoints
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises monotonically with size on all three tasks (e.g. MNLI ours 74.3→83.8%), but no predictive curve is fitted; rows t8-*.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased monotonically across all three tasks and both checkpoint sets, including MNLI from 74.3% to 83.8% for the authors' models, without a predictive fit.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported in-distribution accuracies across MINI, SMALL, MEDIUM, BASE, and LARGE on QQP, MNLI, and SST-2, for both original and study-pretrained checkpoints
reader_labels.reason: Overall downstream accuracy rises across model sizes in the reported comparisons; see rows t8-mini-orig-qqp through t8-large-ours-sst2.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Instance-level correlations conditioned on middle-model accuracy, for the two size triplets in Table 6
reader_labels.reason: The reported correlations are positive in every listed bucket, indicating that gains across successive size steps are associated; see rows t6-sm-mb-010 through t6-mi-ml-100.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Correlation strength across the two MNLI model-size triplets and middle-accuracy buckets
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports correlations become higher when model-size differences are smaller, so the association depends on the size gap; see the SMALL–MEDIUM–BASE and MINI–MEDIUM–LARGE rows t6-sm-mb-010 through t6-mi-ml-100.
